feasible.reason:
The proposal does not defend against the first two of its four named threats, and its headline rationale ("strictly better than Trezor") is inverted on the MCU leg.

Bypass 1 (day-one counterfeit / SWD-emulating fake MCU with transplanted genuine SEs): every pre-first-power check in the proposal (pq1-verify dumping MCU UID, DBGMCU_IDCODE, OTP, FSBL hash) reads values the fake MCU chooses to present over the SWD it emulates; all of them are public or readable at RDP-0 and therefore copyable. The MCU attestation key is created only at first field boot and enrolled by the user on whatever MCU is present, so a fake MCU simply enrols its own key and every later genuine check is self-consistent. The repo itself states why no factory-witnessed per-die MCU key can rescue this under the ship-at-RDP-0 model: DHUK is an ST-substituted constant at RDP-0 and becomes per-die only at RDP>=1 (secure/src/main.rs:760-763, 1496-1499; secure/src/hw/saes.rs:347; secure/src/hw/bhk.rs:475), and gh #249 records "the factory never runs at RDP >= 1, so a per-die DHUK fingerprint is impossible". Trezor's MCU leg (mcu_attestation.c: ML-DSA-44 keypair regenerated per sign from secret_key_mcu_device_auth, pubkey in a factory-provisioned STARTUP_ARGS_TYPE_MCU_DEVICE_CERT) is factory-certified and therefore DOES catch a day-one fake MCU; pq1's owner-enrolled key does not. Owner enrolment removes the factory-held-secret problem but trades away exactly the property the first threat needs. The proposal's own clause "attestation for chip-swap/clone detection only" contradicts its threat line: a clone present at purchase is the case it cannot see.

Bypass 2 (genuine chips moved to a Frankenstein PCB): nothing in the manifest or any proof binds to the PCB. All three genuine chips on a hostile board (display-bus or button implant, tapped I2C) produce an identical UID tuple, pass the vendor chains, pass the owner-enrolled C10 challenge and match the log entry. The proposal flags only "display-bus implant" as unseen, but the Frankenstein-PCB threat is the same thing and is listed as defended.

What survives (real value, but a narrower IMP): (3) factory UID re-use is caught if verifiers enforce tuple uniqueness in the log; (4) per-element binding (each proof to its own root set, identical tuple across all three) is sound and closes the Trezor one-proof-satisfies-all-slots class; and post-enrolment chip substitution (evil-maid swap of the MCU after the owner witnessed att_pk, or SE swap against the logged tuple) is detected, because the RDP-2 DHUK is per-die and unreadable (SAES KEYSEL only). Feasibility of that reduced scope on pq1 is fine: cmac_dhuk (Tier-1 KDF, secure/src/hw/saes_cmac.rs:44) already exists for the KDF root; C10 N=16 gives a 32-B pubkey; code delta is small (C10 sign already linked), OTP has room for a bag serial (512 B, master at 128..160, sentinel 160..176), and the FSBL has ~10 KB of its 38,912 B span free for a serial render.
feasible.corrections:
1. Re-scope the threat line: drop "counterfeit board with SWD-emulating fake MCU" and "genuine chips on a Frankenstein PCB" as defended threats; keep UID re-use, per-element binding, and POST-enrolment chip swap. A day-one fake MCU under ship-at-RDP-0 has no cryptographic detector (DHUK is a shared constant at RDP-0; anything else readable at RDP-0 is copyable) — the only anchors are the physical pre-power SWD readout plus tamper-evident packaging/bag serial, i.e. process, not attestation. If the owner ever wants a Trezor-equivalent MCU leg it requires either factory RDP>=1 (conflicts with the verify-once model, invariant #10) or an MCU-external secret witness; flag that as a design decision, not a firmware task.
2. Rationale fix: "strictly better than Trezor" is wrong for the MCU leg; it is "no factory secret, at the price of no day-one MCU genuineness". State the trade honestly.
3. Timing: on pq1 silicon a genuine check costs a C10 keygen (~1-3 s) + sign (~6.4-7.2 s) each time, since the key is regenerated per use — budget ~10 s per challenge in the companion UX (and the DHUK-rooted seed exists only after Phase A of rdp2-self-lock, so no attestation is possible on a device that has not yet self-locked).
4. Manifest field sha256(otp_area||salt): the OTP area contains the 32-B TRNG per-device master that roots the transport SCP03/admin/PBS credentials (secure/src/hw/otp.rs:45-46). Do not publish a hash of a secret to a public log; hash only non-secret OTP words (bag serial, ship-profile id, sentinel) or hash after the first-boot rotation makes the master dead.
5. Key-purpose fence: a separate KDF label already gives key-level separation from bootstrap/slot/FW keys, so the 'AuthenticateDevice:' prefix is defence-in-depth, not the fence; keep both but do not describe the prefix as load-bearing. The Donjon Safe-3 caveat applies verbatim: a glitched or rogue firmware can use the unreadable DHUK to sign any challenge, so attestation is bounded by FI resistance of the FSBL + first-boot path.
6. Missing readers: secure/src has no OPTIGA 0xE0C2 UID read, no SE050 UID (0x7FFF0206/IDENTIFY) read, and no SE050 attested-read or OPTIGA E0F0 challenge-sign plumbing (grep E0C2/UID in secure/src/{optiga,se050} returns nothing); the manifest and the per-element binding both depend on them. Cost L is right; priority P1 is defensible only for the surviving scope (it is ship-blocker #249's substance), and the proposal is correctly tagged mixed (factory HSM, log operation, OTP burn ceremony).
7. OPTIGA's E0E0 certificate does not self-evidently carry the E0C2 UID; the "identical UID tuple across all three" check needs the MCU's C10 attestation to sign the tuple it read, and SE050's attested read of its own UID object to anchor the SE050 UID — the OPTIGA UID remains MCU-asserted unless an attested read exists for 0xE0C2.

vendor-claim.reason: The precedent claims are substantively true and the 'beyond' novelty claim survives: Trezor Safe 7 (T3W1) does ship a three-chain genuine check with an ML-DSA-44 MCU leg whose keypair is regenerated from a seed on every sign, trezorlib does enforce same-root/same-serial/same-CN across the OPTIGA/TROPIC/MCU chains, the trezor.io advisory confirms the Aug-2026 'proofs verified against a combined key set rather than per secure element' bug on TS7, Ledger's Genuine Check is an SE-held key + HSM challenge-response, Coldcard records the bag number at the factory and shows it on first boot, and Tillitis derives per-device identity from a UDS. No vendor was found that roots the MCU attestation key in a hardware-unique key that does not exist until self-lock (DHUK), enrols it under owner witness, or publishes per-unit manifests to a transparency log — so 'beyond' stands. However several citations are imprecise (wrong line ranges, wrong date attribution for the binding fix, the Trezor MCU root is a factory-era flash-stored TRNG secret rather than hardware-rooted, and the Safe 3 lesson is mis-framed: the Safe 3 had no MCU-held attestation key at all — the issue was an SE-only check passing while the glitched MCU ran modified firmware). Also a pq1 doc claim the proposal leans on ('no shipping wallet currently does triple-UID binding') is stale against Trezor's June-2026 cross-chain serial/CN check.
vendor-claim.corrections: 1) Line ranges: the ML-DSA-44 sign path is core/embed/sec/mcu_attestation/mcu_attestation.c:63-97 (not 45-79); seed via secret_key_mcu_device_auth (:68), mldsa_keypair_internal per call (:74), empty ML-DSA context string (:81-86) so domain separation rests only on the b"AuthenticateDevice:" compact-size-prefixed header built in core/src/apps/management/authenticate_device.py:33-38. The host cross-chain binding is python/src/trezorlib/authentication.py:~683-718 (same root authority; same serial_number; same common_name; CN must start with model internal_name), not 609-700 (that range is the tail of verify_authentication_response plus the per-chain verification calls). 2) Dating: the serial/CN consistency check landed 2026-06-08 (git 9f72b329d8 'Check device certificate CN and SN consistency'); the trezor.io advisory 'Authenticity proofs not bounded to their secure element on TS7' says 'Reported on August 16, 2026', bounty 1350 USD, fix = each proof checked against its own secure element's key set; no CVE, no version named. Whether the 'same root authority' set-equality check in HEAD is that Aug fix was not dated in-tree (no git -S run on that string). 3) Root of Trezor's MCU key: NOT hardware/DHUK-rooted. secret_key_mcu_device_auth = HMAC-SHA256 derivation (secret_keys_common.c:68-96, diversify_and_derive) from SECRET_PRIVILEGED_MASTER_KEY_SLOT 0 (core/embed/models/T3W1/secret_layout.h:61), a flash secret-sector value TRNG-generated on-device by prodtest set_random_secret (core/embed/projects/prodtest/cmd/prodtest_secrets.c:55-88); the ML-DSA pubkey is exported Noise-encrypted to the factory (prodtest_secrets.c:185-220) and the factory-issued cert chain is written back to SECRET_MCU_DEVICE_CERT_OFFSET (core/embed/sec/secret/stm32u5/secret.c:662-675, layout.h:47-48). So 'regenerated per use, never stored' is true of the ML-DSA keypair but the seed root IS stored. This strengthens, not weakens, the pq1 DHUK/owner-enrolled differentiation. 4) Models: USE_MCU_ATTESTATION is enabled in core/embed/models/T3W1/model.toml:15 (Safe 7, mcu=stm32u5g) and T3T2/model.toml:14 (mcu=stm32u58, 'Trezor T3T2', devkit — unreleased internal model). 'Same silicon family' (STM32U5) is right; Safe 7 is U5G, not U585. The trezor.io learn page confirms the May-2026 PQ update moved the MCU 'from a coordinator to a third, independently auditable signature layer'. 5) Donjon/Safe 3 framing: the advisory (reported 2024-11-12) and coverage describe an MCU voltage glitch letting modified firmware run while the OPTIGA-only genuine check still passed; the Safe 3 attestation key lived in the Optiga, not the MCU. Rephrase rationale: 'an SE-only genuine check is only as good as the MCU's glitch resistance / MCU-SE pairing', which is the argument FOR adding an MCU leg, consistent with the design's anchor-on-FSBL-fingerprint stance. 6) Ledger: donjon.ledger.com confirms SE-generated keypair at manufacturing, HSM-signed pubkey ('attestation'), HSM-issued challenge, run on first connect/app install/FW update, explicitly cannot detect implants or supply-chain history — supports the 'None of this sees a display-bus implant' risk line. 7) Coldcard: Coinkite says the bag number is recorded in a 'secure area of flash' (third parties say OTP/SE); 'burned in OTP' should be stated as the pq1 design choice, not the Coldcard precedent. 8) Tillitis: UDS-derived CDI = blake2s(UDS, blake2s(app), USS) is a per-device-identity precedent only; no vendor cert, no attestation key, no genuine-check — cite it for 'identity from a device-unique secret + measurement', not for attestation. 9) Repo evidence all verified: #249 OPEN/NOT STARTED/ship-blocker (notes factory never at RDP>=1 so DHUK fingerprint impossible at factory — the proposal's first-boot derivation is the consistent answer), #68/#67 OPEN ship-blockers, #601 OPEN design-first; secure/src/hw/dbgmcu.rs:1-60 report-only IDCODE; secure/src/die_id.rs pure decode; grep AuthenticateDevice|attestation key|att_sk|pq1-attest in secure/src -> none; docs/hardware/prodtest-receipt-example-pq1.json has only stm32_uid_hex + per-test PASS rows (no SE UIDs, no signature); docs/security/HARDENING.md:410 confirms 'completion-flag check ... not cryptographic per-unit attestation'. 10) Stale pq1 doc: docs/security/production-security.md:347-348 §2.5 says 'no shipping wallet currently does this' (triple-UID binding) — Trezor's shipped trezorlib enforces identical serial/CN across all three chains since 2026-06-08 (weaker than UID-tuple binding, but a cross-chip binding);
